inline_text:
Closes #34.

This PR keeps the sandbox recommendation in Section 3.2 and states what it delivers.

- **Quick start.** Sandbox mode narrows what an unverified artifact can touch from the full user account to the working directory. Unless the boundary is kernel-enforced through filesystem confinement, namespaces, and syscall filtering, it does not close network egress, and it does not cover the handoff to host components that run outside the sandbox. The verification controls stay in place with sandbox mode on.
- **Evidence.** Capsule Security showed the egress gap on an ordinary task in Cursor: the sandbox proxy refused the agent's curl upload, so the agent reached the internet through a Python HTTP client the sandbox did not cover and uploaded project files to a public anonymous host: https://www.capsulesecurity.io/blog-post/cursebox-the-agent-that-sends-your-files-to-strangers-to-get-the-job-done. Pillar Security reproduced escapes across Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, and Antigravity, and in almost every case the agent wrote a file that a trusted component outside the sandbox later ran: https://www.pillar.security/blog/the-week-of-sandbox-escapes. Both get ledger rows.
- **Environment risk table.** The sandbox row changes from "Contained" to "Narrowed", and network access reads "Allowlisted at the proxy", which is where the allowlist applies.

The Last Modified line in deliverables/README.md is also touched by #38, #39, and #40, which is a one-line fix for whichever merges later.

Disclosure: I work at Capsule Security, which published the first post above, and I co-lead the spec workstream of the OWASP Agent Control Standard, which is not cited here.

@MatthewKhouzam @flucktemberg-sap this is the PR for #34.
